_Dear Readers:_
_Some of the most meaningful work of my career has been alongside Indigenous communities fighting to preserve their lands, histories, and ways of life. Those experiences profoundly shaped how I understand geography, science, and our responsibility to the people whose stories have too often been erased._
_This Indigenous Peoples ' Day, I'm sharing the extraordinary work of artists and cartographers who are reclaiming those stories, one map at a time._
_Mesoscale News exists to tell the stories that deserve more attention, especially when they challenge the powerful, confront uncomfortable histories, or give voice to communities too often ignored.**If you believe in journalism grounded in science, guided by compassion, and unafraid to speak truth to power, please consider becoming a paid subscriber.** Your support makes this work possible._
* * *
_On Indigenous Peoples ' Day, the artists and geographers restoring the histories that colonization erased, and why the fight to map Indigenous homelands is inseparable from the global struggle for land, identity, and survival._
Years ago, deep in the [disappearing wetlands](https://substack.com/redirect/e924534e-618d-4736-a40b-960cb385a12e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) of coastal Louisiana, I stood alongside Indigenous tribal leaders searching for places that, according to the maps, did not exist.
Burial grounds. Ancestral settlements. Sacred places. Landscapes that had carried generations of history, only to be omitted from the official geographic record.
I was working with the [Pointe-au-Chien Indian Tribe](https://substack.com/redirect/a2c826a6-4ebf-4ed8-97bd-55db892fd819?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) and the [Isle de Jean Charles](https://substack.com/redirect/22f1fdde-b50d-40e5-a78b-7b052ada71e6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), documenting historical sites and studying how hurricanes, rising seas, and centuries of environmental change had reshaped their homelands.
My research in Louisiana eventually [became my Ph.D. work](https://substack.com/redirect/ccfd1f4d-6b41-474e-9436-b3e747bc4720?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), examining how Indigenous settlement patterns, burial practices, and oral histories could preserve evidence of catastrophic weather events long before modern meteorological records existed.
What began as an exercise in geographic science became something far more profound.
The absence of a place from a map does not mean it was never there. Sometimes it means the people who knew it were never asked. Sometimes the records were destroyed, the names changed, or the knowledge passed between generations in ways Western institutions never learned to recognize.
And sometimes, the people making the maps had every reason to pretend the land was empty.
The communities I worked with were fighting to preserve far more than their physical homes. They were trying to protect the places where their ancestors were buried, where their histories were written into the landscape, and where generations had learned to live with the water rather than against it.
But the water was rising. The marshes were disappearing. And many of those places had never been formally documented.
_**What happens when a people lose their land before the rest of the world has even acknowledged their history on it?**_
That question has stayed with me throughout my career.
And this Indigenous Peoples' Day, I want to introduce you to some extraordinary artists, cartographers, and geographers whose work confronts that question from a different direction.
They are restoring Indigenous names to rivers and mountains. Reconstructing the geographies of nations that existed long before the United States and Canada. Transforming maps into works of art that challenge centuries of dispossession.
Their work is beautiful. It is scientifically and historically important. And it is part of a much larger struggle over who gets to define a place, who belongs to it, and who has the right to decide its future.
* * *
## **Before the Borders, There Were Nations**
For thousands of years before European colonization, North America was home to hundreds of distinct Indigenous nations, with their own languages, political systems, agricultural traditions, trade networks, spiritual geographies, and relationships to the land.
The continent was neither empty nor waiting to be discovered.
Yet colonial maps frequently portrayed Indigenous homelands as territories available for occupation, acquisition, and exploitation. Native place names were replaced. Communities were omitted or displaced. Political boundaries were imposed without the consent of the people who lived there.
Maps became instruments of administration, property ownership, military expansion, and colonial authority.
The consequences extend far beyond the historical record.
A map that fails to recognize an Indigenous nation's relationship to its homeland can shape decisions about land ownership, resource extraction, conservation, infrastructure, and displacement.
And the people whose history has been erased from the map may then be forced to prove that history existed at all.
* * *
## **Marlena Myles: A Homeland Written in Dakota**
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/50e88ea0-21b9-4214-80ea-9ac2b3877bdf?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
[Explore Marlena Myles' Dakota Land Maps](https://substack.com/redirect/c8590d55-5b78-44fd-a5cb-9f788173151c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Artist Marlena Myles creates richly illustrated maps that restore Dakota names, stories, and cultural knowledge to the landscapes of Minnesota.
Her _Dakota Land Maps_ , developed with Dakota-language contributions from Dawi, reveal a geography far older than the cities and state boundaries imposed upon it. Rivers, trails, and sacred places emerge through Indigenous language and memory.
These are more than historical reconstructions. They're living expressions of Dakota identity, reminding us that Indigenous peoples are not relics of the past. Their histories, languages, and relationships to the land endure.
* * *
## **Margaret Wickens Pearce: The Stories Hidden in Place Names**
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/36ed0090-8b13-41f7-9efd-ee1513ddc6af?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
[Explore ](https://substack.com/redirect/4f083f5b-6f91-44f3-8144-83c2c53845b5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_[Coming Home to Indigenous Place Names in Canada](https://substack.com/redirect/4f083f5b-6f91-44f3-8144-83c2c53845b5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_
Cartographer Margaret Wickens Pearce restores Indigenous geography by returning its original names and stories to the map.
Her _Coming Home to Indigenous Place Names in Canada_ , created with Indigenous contributors, reveals how colonial naming practices obscured generations of cultural and ecological knowledge.
A place name can preserve the memory of a migration, describe a river's behavior, or identify resources that sustained communities for centuries. Pearce's work reminds us that changing a name can obscure far more than a location. It can obscure an entire way of understanding the world.
* * *
## **Aaron Carapella: A Continent of Nations**
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/41aae4bb-4c8d-4e45-8cc4-1b6168fd7665?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
[Explore Tribal Nations Maps](https://substack.com/redirect/73699116-e3ed-41e3-a220-913a0bebe1f6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Aaron Carapella's _Tribal Nations Maps_ replaces the familiar political geography of North America with the names and homelands of hundreds of Indigenous nations.
Drawing on historical research, his maps challenge the notion that the continent was an empty wilderness awaiting European settlement.
No single map can perfectly reconstruct centuries of shifting territories and overlapping relationships to land. But Carapella's work makes something unmistakable: long before the United States and Canada existed, this continent was already home to complex societies, political systems, and thriving nations.
* * *
## **Jaune Quick-to-See Smith: A Map of What Was Taken**
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/933b0eb5-d871-4f39-9b60-f4c96342da86?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
[Explore Smith's work at the National Gallery of Art](https://substack.com/redirect/b61c59bc-6d44-460b-b127-6a77c41ef0de?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Artist Jaune Quick-to-See Smith transformed familiar American maps into powerful examinations of Indigenous dispossession and cultural erasure.
In _State Names_ (2000), she removed state names without Indigenous linguistic origins, exposing how colonial geography has obscured the continent's earlier histories.
Her work asks us to reconsider the authority of the borders and names we take for granted--and whose stories were displaced to make them appear permanent
* * *
## **Christi Belcourt: Painting the Geography That Maps Leave Out**
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/8c973289-619d-489c-afec-1ebe8fc5a979?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
[Explore Christi Belcourt's work](https://substack.com/redirect/e201f394-9767-4832-b01e-83efd1b551e2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Metis artist Christi Belcourt explores the relationships between Indigenous identity, land, and ecological knowledge through richly detailed paintings.
Her Mapping Roots: Perspectives of Land & Water in Ontario series combines contemporary maps with Indigenous place names and cultural imagery, revealing relationships to the landscape that conventional cartography rarely captures.
Belcourt's work reminds us that land is more than property or a collection of resources. It is memory, culture, identity, and an inheritance that cannot simply be relocated or replaced.
* * *
## **Mapping as a Human Right**
The struggle to restore Indigenous geography is not confined to North America.
Across the world, Indigenous peoples are using maps to defend their homelands against deforestation, mining, oil development, displacement, and the accelerating consequences of climate change.
In the Amazon, community-led mapping initiatives have documented ancestral territories, traditional resource use, sacred places, and environmental damage.
These maps can help communities establish evidence of customary land use, organize territorial management, and defend their rights in legal and political proceedings.
The [Amazon Conservation Team](https://substack.com/redirect/a739e8b6-4397-4aab-a71b-79e33e251ca8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) works with Indigenous communities on participatory mapping and biocultural conservation.
Brazil's [New Social Mapping in the Amazon](https://substack.com/redirect/51bdb23b-8640-4c04-a0fc-b566102b8694?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) initiative has supported communities in producing their own maps, using GPS and locally defined geographic knowledge to document land use and strengthen territorial protections.
In the Peruvian Amazon, community mapping has similarly helped document Indigenous relationships with forests and waterways while supporting efforts to defend traditional territories.
The parallels with coastal Louisiana are unmistakable.
Indigenous peoples are frequently expected to demonstrate their historical relationship to lands that their ancestors occupied long before modern property systems existed.
Their oral histories, ecological knowledge, and cultural practices may contain precisely the evidence needed to establish those relationships.
But those forms of knowledge have not always been afforded the same authority as written colonial records, government surveys, or property deeds.
This creates a devastating contradiction: communities can be required to prove their connection to their own homelands using systems of documentation developed by the governments that dispossessed them.
Mapping can help challenge that imbalance.
But there is another danger.
When Indigenous communities document sacred sites, burial grounds, culturally sensitive landscapes, or valuable ecological resources, making that information public can expose those places to exploitation, vandalism, or further dispossession.
The goal cannot simply be to put everything on a map.
**It must be to give Indigenous peoples authority over what is mapped, how that knowledge is used, and who is allowed to see it.**
That is the difference between mapping Indigenous lands and supporting Indigenous sovereignty.
[Working with Palestinians in the West Bank](https://substack.com/redirect/2c182a3e-5b92-4464-8071-22ec2cdc355e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) parallels much of my work in Louisiana: Generations beyond memory of people working a land being stolen from them, not because of hurricanes and climate change, but through administrative processes, being led by a foreign terror campaign, funded by the United States.
* * *
## **The Arctic: When the Maps Can No Longer Keep Up**
Thousands of miles north of Louisiana, Inuit communities are confronting another consequence of a rapidly changing climate: the sea ice is changing.
Routes used for generations are becoming less predictable. Seasonal patterns are shifting. Knowledge of currents, winds, wildlife, and ice conditions is increasingly important for understanding both the changes underway and their consequences for Arctic communities.
Inuit knowledge systems contain extraordinarily detailed understandings of these environments.
Through projects such as [SIKU](https://substack.com/redirect/dcf713b8-3a46-4438-b0ea-11a9db653096?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) and the [Inuinnait Knowledge Atlases](https://substack.com/redirect/425ac02e-a29e-4bee-9f84-d3d8c38eb1d3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), Indigenous communities and collaborators are bringing traditional knowledge into digital mapping platforms.
These projects document travel routes, geographic names, environmental observations, and cultural histories while supporting the transmission of knowledge between generations.
The maps are not simply records of the past-- they are tools for navigating a changing present, and they challenge a persistent assumption in Western science: that meaningful environmental data began when modern instruments started recording it.
Indigenous peoples have observed changing landscapes for thousands of years.
Their knowledge is not a substitute for satellite measurements, climate models, or field observations. It is another essential body of evidence, often describing environmental relationships and historical conditions that instruments alone cannot capture.
For someone whose career has centered on climate science and geospatial analysis, that lesson is fundamental.
The most useful map is not necessarily the one containing the most data, it's the one that helps us understand the world more completely.
* * *
## **The Right to Land Is the Right to a Future**
In 2007, the United Nations adopted the [Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples](https://substack.com/redirect/1b746402-fba6-4bfd-a3ab-52673f1485f6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), establishing international standards for the protection of Indigenous cultures, identities, institutions, and relationships to their traditional territories.
Article 26 recognizes Indigenous peoples' rights to lands, territories, and resources they have traditionally owned, occupied, or used.
Article 32 addresses their right to determine priorities for development and requires governments to consult and cooperate in good faith to obtain free, prior, and informed consent before approving projects affecting those territories.
These are not abstract principles.
They speak directly to disputes over mines, pipelines, dams, logging concessions, conservation areas, and development projects around the world.
They also speak to climate adaptation.
When an Indigenous community is threatened by rising seas, relocation is not merely a question of moving houses to higher ground.
Who selects the new location? Who controls the land? Can the community remain together? What happens to ancestral burial grounds and sacred places? Who determines which traditions and relationships can be maintained?
I watched versions of these questions unfold during my work with the Isle de Jean Charles community in Louisiana.
The tribe became internationally known through discussions of climate displacement and a state-led relocation initiative. But the process also raised serious questions about [consultation, cultural continuity, and who should have authority over decisions affecting the community's future.](https://substack.com/redirect/8713b67c-7258-473d-a51f-d60b52b47df1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Those questions remain relevant wherever Indigenous peoples face displacement, whether from climate change, resource extraction, infrastructure development, or state policies.
The United Nations has repeatedly warned that Indigenous peoples continue to face barriers to securing their territorial rights, even as the lands they inhabit contain some of the world's most ecologically significant environments.
The [LandMark global Indigenous and community land-rights platform](https://substack.com/redirect/a9dc2c59-213e-458c-bbec-1f520dc0e42b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) makes another problem visible: substantial portions of lands held or used by Indigenous peoples and local communities remain absent from available mapping datasets.
That absence does not mean those lands are unoccupied.
It means our records remain incomplete.
And incomplete records can have very real consequences for the people whose rights depend on being recognized.
* * *
## **The Land Remembers**
I still think about the places we documented along the Louisiana coast.
Some were visible in the landscape. Others required listening to tribal elders, studying historical records, examining aerial imagery, and understanding how the land had changed over generations.
We were not discovering those places; the people whose ancestors had lived there already knew them.
We were working to translate that knowledge into forms that institutions accustomed to maps, coordinates, and technical documentation might finally recognize.
Indigenous communities do not need scientists, historians, or cartographers to tell them that their histories are real.
They need their knowledge respected, their rights recognized, and their authority over their own homelands upheld.
That is what connects the work of Marlena Myles, Margaret Wickens Pearce, Aaron Carapella, Jaune Quick-to-See Smith, Christi Belcourt, and Indigenous mapping initiatives around the world.
Their maps are not simply attempts to recreate a world that existed before colonization -- they are expressions of a world that still exists.
A world of languages that survived efforts to extinguish them. Of communities that survived forced removal. Of histories preserved in stories, waterways, burial grounds, and place names. Of peoples whose relationships with their homelands cannot be erased by drawing new boundaries over them.
On Indigenous Peoples' Day, we should celebrate the beauty and brilliance of that work.
But we should also recognize what is at stake.
Because when a community loses its land, it may lose places that cannot be recreated anywhere else. When a language disappears, entire systems of geographic and ecological knowledge can disappear with it. And when a sacred place is destroyed, no amount of money can restore the generations of memory it held.
The maps we use shape how we understand the world, influence what we protect, what we exploit, whose claims we recognize, and whose histories we consider worth preserving.
As a geographer, I have spent much of my life studying how landscapes change.
As someone who has worked alongside Indigenous communities fighting to preserve their homelands, I have also learned that the most important question is not always what has changed.
Sometimes it is what we have chosen not to see.

Sacred places. Landscapes that had carried generations of history, only to be omitted from the official geographic record. I was working with the and the , documenting historical sites and studying how hurricanes, rising seas, and centuries of environmental change had reshaped their homelands. My research in Louisiana eventually , examining how Indigenous settlement patterns, burial practices, and oral histories could preserve evidence of catastrophic weather events long before modern meteorological records existed. What began as an exercise in geographic science became something far more profound. The absence of a place from a map does not mean it was never there. Sometimes it means the people who knew it were never asked. Sometimes the records were destroyed, the names changed, or the knowledge passed between generations in ways Western institutions never learned to recognize. And sometimes, the people making the maps had every reason to pretend the land was empty. The communities I worked with were fighting to preserve far more than their physical homes. They were trying to protect the places where their ancestors were buried, where their histories were written into the landscape, and where generations had learned to live with the water rather than against it. But the water was rising. The marshes were disappearing. And many of those places had never been formally documented. The continent was neither empty nor waiting to be discovered. Yet colonial maps frequently portrayed Indigenous homelands as territories available for occupation, acquisition, and exploitation. Native place names were replaced. Communities were omitted or displaced. Political boundaries were imposed without the consent of the people who lived there. Maps became instruments of administration, property ownership, military expansion, and colonial authority. The consequences extend far beyond the historical record. A map that fails to recognize an Indigenous nation's relationship to its homeland can shape decisions about land ownership, resource extraction, conservation, infrastructure, and displacement. And the people whose history has been erased from the map may then be forced to prove that history existed at all. Marlena Myles: A Homeland Written in Dakota | | ---|---|--- Artist Marlena Myles creates richly illustrated maps that restore Dakota names, stories, and cultural knowledge to the landscapes of Minnesota. Her Dakota Land Maps , developed with Dakota-language contributions from Dawi, reveal a geography far older than the cities and state boundaries imposed upon it. Rivers, trails, and sacred places emerge through Indigenous language and memory. These are more than historical reconstructions. They're living expressions of Dakota identity, reminding us that Indigenous peoples are not relics of the past. Their histories, languages, and relationships to the land endure. Margaret Wickens Pearce: The Stories Hidden in Place Names | | ---|---|--- Cartographer Margaret Wickens Pearce restores Indigenous geography by returning its original names and stories to the map. Her Coming Home to Indigenous Place Names in Canada , created with Indigenous contributors, reveals how colonial naming practices obscured generations of cultural and ecological knowledge. A place name can preserve the memory of a migration, describe a river's behavior, or identify resources that sustained communities for centuries. Pearce's work reminds us that changing a name can obscure far more than a location. It can obscure an entire way of understanding the world. Aaron Carapella: A Continent of Nations | | ---|---|--- Aaron Carapella's Tribal Nations Maps replaces the familiar political geography of North America with the names and homelands of hundreds of Indigenous nations. Drawing on historical research, his maps challenge the notion that the continent was an empty wilderness awaiting European settlement. No single map can perfectly reconstruct centuries of shifting territories and overlapping relationships to land. But Carapella's work makes something unmistakable: long before the United States and Canada existed, this continent was already home to complex societies, political systems, and thriving nations. Jaune Quick-to-See Smith: A Map of What Was Taken | | ---|---|--- Artist Jaune Quick-to-See Smith transformed familiar American maps into powerful examinations of Indigenous dispossession and cultural erasure. In State Names (2000), she removed state names without Indigenous linguistic origins, exposing how colonial geography has obscured the continent's earlier histories. Her Mapping Roots: Perspectives of Land & Water in Ontario series combines contemporary maps with Indigenous place names and cultural imagery, revealing relationships to the landscape that conventional cartography rarely captures. Belcourt's work reminds us that land is more than property or a collection of resources. It is memory, culture, identity, and an inheritance that cannot simply be relocated or replaced. Across the world, Indigenous peoples are using maps to defend their homelands against deforestation, mining, oil development, displacement, and the accelerating consequences of climate change. **1\. The claim**
Viral posts assert that "lawyers get taxpayer money to assist immigration" -- that public funds pay attorneys to help migrants enter or remain in the United States, and that this spending sustains the immigration bar. The claim is partially true, but mostly in the past tense, and it misattributes the largest source of immigration-lawyer income. Here is the documented picture.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/35701ddb-eee4-4535-8069-647ff64c8a58?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
**2\. The legal baseline**
In U.S. immigration court there is **no constitutional right to appointed counsel** ; _Gideon_ does not apply to civil removal proceedings. Any government-funded legal help has therefore existed only through specifically appropriated programs -- information services, limited representation, and court-mandated representation for narrow classes of people. General civil legal-aid money (Legal Services Corporation grants) is separately restricted by federal law and cannot pay for most representation of undocumented immigrants.
**3\. What taxpayers actually funded, and for how long**
> • **DOJ/EOIR legal-access programs.** The Executive Office for Immigration Review funded the Legal Orientation Program (LOP), its family and custodian variants (FGLOP/LOPC), the Immigration Court Helpdesk (ICH), and the Counsel for Children Initiative (CCI) -- group "know your rights" sessions, courthouse help desks, and children's legal services delivered by nonprofit contractors. DOJ's own FY2026 budget justification acknowledged the LOP "costs taxpayers tens of millions of dollars each year," while arguing it produced "no return on investment."
> • **The National Qualified Representative Program (NQRP).** Government-paid representatives for unaccompanied children and respondents found mentally incompetent -- the narrowest category, rooted in case law and regulation. This program continues; a Congressional Research Service analysis notes EOIR's replacement "Public Resources Program" still includes it.
> • **HHS/ORR legal services for unaccompanied children.** The largest federal line item: a contract with the Acacia Center for Justice, funded at roughly **$200 million** (HHS described it at about $20 million per month), covering legal screenings, orientation, and -- for a period -- direct representation for thousands of children.
> • **State and local funds.** New York's FY2026 budget allocated **$64.2 million** for immigration legal services (advocates had sought $175 million), and other states run similar programs.
So the core of the viral claim is accurate for the period through mid-2025: taxpayer money did pay immigration lawyers and legal-aid nonprofits at meaningful scale.
**4\. What changed in 2025 -2026**
> • **April 2025:** DOJ ordered stop-work and terminated the EOIR legal-access programs -- LOP, FGLOP, LOPC, ICH, and CCI -- effective April 16, 2025, "for the convenience of the government" (per DOJ termination notices and the Acacia Center's own statement).
> • **March 2025:** The Office of Refugee Resettlement moved to terminate the direct-representation portion of the Acacia contract, which the provider estimated served about 26,000 children.
> • **July 31, 2026:** The remaining ~$200M HHS-Acacia contract **expired**. NPR reported that more than 24,000 children nationwide lost services. House Appropriations Democrats and NPR reported the administration declined to extend the contract unless the nonprofit agreed to hand over sensitive case information about the children; that characterization has not been confirmed by the administration.
> • **State backfill:** New York executed **$7.25 million** in contracts to preserve legal services for roughly 1,400 affected children -- a partial, state-funded substitute for the lapsed federal program.
> • **The counter-trend:** the July 2025 reconciliation act added tens of billions of dollars for ICE enforcement and detention, plus billions more for expanded immigration-court capacity. EOIR's enacted budget nonetheless fell from about **$844 million (FY2025) to $800 million (FY2026)**.
The net effect: by October 2026, most federal funding for _non-government_ lawyers helping immigrants has been terminated or allowed to lapse. What remains is NQRP, state programs like New York's, and pro bono work (EOIR maintains a public List of Pro Bono Legal Service Providers, last updated September 24, 2026).
**5\. The policy debate, stated fairly**
**Critics of the spending** (including DOJ's FY2026 justification) argue the programs rewarded unlawful presence, prolonged cases, and delivered no measurable return. **Defenders** point to program evaluations finding that orientation and representation improved hearing-appearance rates, sped up dockets, and reduced detention days -- arguing the programs cost less than the enforcement resources they saved. The sharpest dispute involves children: whether due-process representation for minors is a cheap safeguard or an inducement to unlawful migration. Both sides cite real dollar figures; they disagree about what the money bought.
**6\. Where the viral framing is misdirected: Big Law and the H-1B pipeline**
The claim's weakest link is the implication that immigration lawyers generally live off taxpayer money. The largest immigration-law payrolls are paid by **employers, not appropriations** :
> • Survey data of Vault 100 firms indicates roughly **86% of large corporate firms are willing to sponsor H-1B candidates** -- about 39% outright and 47% case-by-case -- with green-card sponsorship typically arriving around an associate's **sixth year** , tied to partnership decisions.
> • Firms such as **Fragomen, Berry Appleman & Leiden, and Ogletree Deakins** file tens of thousands of Labor Condition Applications annually -- but as **outside counsel for corporate clients who pay the fees**. The LCA is an employer filing with the Department of Labor; the sponsorship costs, prevailing-wage obligations, and legal bills all fall on the employer.
> • The sector disparity noted in the same materials -- small and public-interest firms rarely sponsor -- reflects the cost (sponsorship can run well into five figures, plus annual lottery risk) and explains the bar's two-tier structure: a wealthy corporate practice funded by clients, and a grant-funded or charitable legal-aid sector that taxpayers once subsidized and now largely do not.
> • Current context: a proposed six-figure H-1B fee (reported at approximately $103,265) is further reshaping the economics of sponsorship for firms and employers alike.
None of this pipeline touches taxpayer money. If anything, the government now collects more from the H-1B system than it spends on it.
**7\. The J-1 thread, kept separate**
On October 8, 2026 an announcement by Vice President Vance and Labor Secretary Sonderling of an investigation, with subpoenas, into nine universities -- including Arizona State -- over alleged J-1 misuse that undercuts American researchers. That is a distinct issue: it concerns universities' use of an exchange-visa program, it is an **investigation rather than a finding of wrongdoing** , and it involves no allegation of lawyer funding. The "taxpayer lawyers" narrative and the J-1 narrative circulate together online but have separate factual records.
**8\. Bottom line**
> • For years, taxpayers funded immigration legal help at real scale -- "tens of millions" annually on EOIR programs by DOJ's own account, a ~$200M contract for children's legal services, and state funds like New York's $64.2M.
> • Most of that architecture is now gone. The EOIR programs were terminated in April 2025; the children's-services contract lapsed July 31, 2026; what remains is NQRP, state backfills, and charity.
> • The biggest immigration-law practices -- Fragomen, BAL, Ogletree, and the Big Law H-1B machine -- are paid by employers, never by taxpayers.
> • Taxpayer money still pays immigration lawyers in volume, but overwhelmingly on the government side -- DOJ trial attorneys and ICE counsel -- whose funding grew as the aid programs died.
Read accurately, the claim describes a system that existed until 2025 and has since been largely dismantled -- while the private, employer-funded half of the immigration bar, which the viral posts often point to as evidence, was never taxpayer-funded at all.

EOIR's enacted budget nonetheless fell from about $844 million (FY2025) to $800 million (FY2026). The net effect: by October 2026, most federal funding for non-government lawyers helping immigrants has been terminated or allowed to lapse. What remains is NQRP, state programs like New York's, and pro bono work (EOIR maintains a public List of Pro Bono Legal Service Providers, last updated September 24, 2026). 5\. The policy debate, stated fairly Critics of the spending (including DOJ's FY2026 justification) argue the programs rewarded unlawful presence, prolonged cases, and delivered no measurable return. Defenders point to program evaluations finding that orientation and representation improved hearing-appearance rates, sped up dockets, and reduced detention days -- arguing the programs cost less than the enforcement resources they saved. The sharpest dispute involves children: whether due-process representation for minors is a cheap safeguard or an inducement to unlawful migration. Both sides cite real dollar figures; they disagree about what the money bought. 6\. Where the viral framing is misdirected: Big Law and the H-1B pipeline The claim's weakest link is the implication that immigration lawyers generally live off taxpayer money. The largest immigration-law payrolls are paid by employers, not appropriations : • Survey data of Vault 100 firms indicates roughly 86% of large corporate firms are willing to sponsor H-1B candidates -- about 39% outright and 47% case-by-case -- with green-card sponsorship typically arriving around an associate's sixth year , tied to partnership decisions. • Firms such as Fragomen, Berry Appleman & Leiden, and Ogletree Deakins file tens of thousands of Labor Condition Applications annually -- but as outside counsel for corporate clients who pay the fees. The LCA is an employer filing with the Department of Labor; the sponsorship costs, prevailing-wage obligations, and legal bills all fall on the employer. • The sector disparity noted in the same materials -- small and public-interest firms rarely sponsor -- reflects the cost (sponsorship can run well into five figures, plus annual lottery risk) and explains the bar's two-tier structure: a wealthy corporate practice funded by clients, and a grant-funded or charitable legal-aid sector that taxpayers once subsidized and now largely do not. • Current context: a proposed six-figure H-1B fee (reported at approximately $103,265) is further reshaping the economics of sponsorship for firms and employers alike. None of this pipeline touches taxpayer money. If anything, the government now collects more from the H-1B system than it spends on it. 7\. The J-1 thread, kept separate On October 8, 2026 an announcement by Vice President Vance and Labor Secretary Sonderling of an investigation, with subpoenas, into nine universities -- including Arizona State -- over alleged J-1 misuse that undercuts American researchers. That is a distinct issue: it concerns universities' use of an exchange-visa program, it is an investigation rather than a finding of wrongdoing , and it involves no allegation of lawyer funding. The "taxpayer lawyers" narrative and the J-1 narrative circulate together online but have separate factual records. 8\. Bottom line • For years, taxpayers funded immigration legal help at real scale -- "tens of millions" annually on EOIR programs by DOJ's own account, a ~$200M contract for children's legal services, and state funds like New York's $64.2M. • Most of that architecture is now gone. The EOIR programs were terminated in April 2025; the children's-services contract lapsed July 31, 2026; what remains is NQRP, state backfills, and charity. • The biggest immigration-law practices -- Fragomen, BAL, Ogletree, and the Big Law H-1B machine -- are paid by employers, never by taxpayers. • Taxpayer money still pays immigration lawyers in volume, but overwhelmingly on the government side -- DOJ trial attorneys and ICE counsel -- whose funding grew as the aid programs died. Read accurately, the claim describes a system that existed until 2025 and has since been largely dismantled -- while the private, employer-funded half of the immigration bar, which the viral posts often point to as evidence, was never taxpayer-funded at all. Hi Peter,

Election Day is just over three weeks away, but this race is being decided
right now. Let me explain:

A majority of Michiganders cast their vote before Election Day, either by
mail or through early voting. Absentee ballots are already landing on
kitchen counters across the state.

So when I think about how much time we have left to reach undecided
voters, I'm not counting down to November 3. For a lot of folks, that
decision is happening today, tomorrow, and all throughout October.

[ https://act.abdulformichigan.com/go/507?c0=em-ms-aes-20261012-2-ak._3Ht2J&amount=10&refcode=em20261012-3486&t=1004&akid=3526%2E251025%2ECCDo8R ]Can you chip in $10 or any amount right now so that we
can reach voters while their ballots are still blank?

There's also an upcoming deadline we need to focus on.

October 14, this Wednesday, marks our last pre-election FEC filing
deadline. Every federal campaign has to publicly report what it raised and
what it has left to spend.

Republican strategists read these reports closely. If our numbers are
strong, it tells Mike Rogers’ mega-donors that this seat won't come cheap.
If they're weak, they'll take it as a signal to pour in a few million
more.

So a $10 donation before October 14 does two jobs:

1. It puts our message in front of a voter holding a ballot.
2. It puts a number on our final pre-election FEC report that makes the
MAGA billionaires betting against us think twice.

I don't take corporate PAC money. I never have, and I never will. The only
way we’ll reach the voters we need to win and hit our $6 million
pre-election FEC deadline goal is if folks like you step up to support our
campaign.

[ https://act.abdulformichigan.com/go/507?c0=em-ms-aes-20261012-2-ak._3Ht2J&amount=10&refcode=em20261012-3486&t=1005&akid=3526%2E251025%2ECCDo8R ]Peter, will

Abdul

Friend, Donald Trump’s fascism and abuse of power has now come to my literal front door.
**This morning, DHS agents raided and searched my home in the DC area as the latest step in their ludicrous, partisan investigation into my immigration status.**
I have been in Trump’s crosshairs for years, but now he is escalating in a desperate attempt to drag me and the entire progressive movement down ahead of the midterms.
[**This is a critical moment for our democracy, and we must be decisive. Please, stand by me and our movement today by rushing a contribution to help me fight back in the face of Trump’s abuse of power >>**](https://act.ilhanomar.com/go/7?c0=io-em-dhs-oct26.4A7Axt&refcode=em261012-1-210&t=3&akid=2510%2E791427%2EA03gve)

It’s no accident that this raid comes three weeks before an election where I’m on the ballot.
This is part of the fascist playbook to rile up Trump’s die-hard supporters and give them a big distraction in advance of the midterms. With this obviously political investigation, Trump is telling his voters: **‘Ignore the price of gas, ignore the war in Iran, ignore that you’re losing your healthcare — we want you to get angry about _this_ instead.”**
Throughout his presidency, Trump has weaponized the DOJ to target his political opponents, manufacturing charges that have been roundly dismissed by court after court. And I’m not even the first member of Congress to be targeted. The point is to waste everyone’s time and resources, and generate negative headlines for his opponents.
**I will repeat what I have long said: This is a sham investigation, and Trump’s escalation is only further proof that he is willing to use the power of the federal government to try to intimidate and silence anyone who stands up to him. It’s up to us to make sure it doesn’t work.**

name: Gina Hinojosa
subject: Did you get the memo?
body:
# [](https://ginafortexas.com/?refcode=em_ms_gh_header)[](https://ginafortexas.com/?refcode=em_ms_gh_header)
Hi, Peter — it's Gina.
Everywhere I go in Texas, I hear the same thing: people are struggling in ways they've never struggled before. Working people donating plasma before their shift just to cover the bills. Families rationing insulin. Small businesses closing because property taxes have gotten so out of hand.
And everywhere I go, _I hear something else too: that this movement is giving them hope._ We’re closer than we’ve ever been before, but we have a long way to go. People still worry if we can actually win here.
I understand that skepticism. Democrats have been saying Texas is turning for years. **But something is different now, and I need you to see the numbers.**
My campaign manager Amy put together a memo on exactly where this race stands. Four independent polls now show us ahead. Abbott's own strategist is admitting it will be close. Conservatives across Texas are crossing over — on schools, on data centers, on the simple question of whether this state belongs to the people or to Greg Abbott's billionaire donors.
**[Read the memo. Then, if you believe what I believe — that we can actually win this — I'm asking you to pitch in whatever you can.](https://act.ginafortexas.com/go/1356?c0=em_ms_gh_20261012_2_memo.mPsRb1&refcode=em20261012-2390&t=1&akid=2390%2E299639%2E85G_us)**
[Donate »](https://act.ginafortexas.com/go/1356?c0=em_ms_gh_20261012_2_memo.mPsRb1&refcode=em20261012-2390&t=2&akid=2390%2E299639%2E85G_us)
=============================================================
**OCTOBER 2026 CAMPAIGN MEMO ON TX-GOV**
**FROM:** Amy Friedman, Campaign Manager, Gina for Texas
**TO:** Interested Parties
Let me tell you where this race actually stands — because what's happening in Texas right now is something I don't think the national establishment fully understands yet.

**Gina Hinojosa is leading Greg Abbott in four of the most recent polls. That’s never happened before.**
This race is closer than ever but some people still don’t believe we can win — that’s exactly why I'm writing this memo. And it's exactly why this race could slip away if we don't act.
Here's the polling picture. This race has moved steadily and dramatically in Gina's direction since the spring:
* Texas Politics Project (April 2026): Abbott +5
* TPOR (July 2026): Abbott +3, inside the margin of error
* N+ Univision (September 9): Tied 47–47, with Gina leading Latino voters by 12
* ReconMR/Siena (September 17): **Gina leads 49–45** — independents breaking for Gina 65–27
* NPR/Marist (September 23): **Gina leads 49–46** , winning independents 52–39, pulling 9% of self-identified Republicans
* NYT/Siena (October 4): **Gina leads 49–46** , winning independents 55–39, and leading among Latino voters by 31 points
* YouGov (October 2026): Gina +1

Both RealClearPolitics and Nate Silver's Silver Bulletin have the polling average under 2 points. This is a toss-up.
**Abbott is outspending us 10 to 1 — and he still isn’t getting the result he wants.**
Between July 30 and September 8 alone, Abbott outspent Gina $28 million to $2 million on advertising. Over the full race, he's spent $47 million to our $5 million. Despite that, Gina leads in four of the most recent polls. Abbott's favorability has gone deeply negative — 45% favorable, 53% unfavorable — and his job approval has flipped the same way. He's even polling 13% unfavorable among his own Republicans.
Abbott is a damaged incumbent with a nine-figure war chest. The only thing keeping this race from breaking open is the spending gap.
But here’s the truth: The more money Abbott spends lying about Gina’s record, the more vulnerable we are. _We have to raise more money to reach the voters who haven’t heard from us yet._
**Something real is happening on the ground — and Republicans know it.**
Lifelong conservative voters are publicly breaking with Abbott over two issues.
On education: conservative moms who backed Abbott before are now appearing at Gina's events, frustrated by a decade of voucher schemes and defunded public schools. Gina is running an ad featuring a self-described MAGA conservative who protested on January 6 — and is now voting for Gina because of schools.
On data centers: rural Republican protest groups — including one in Lubbock led by Republicans — are furious about unregulated expansion driving up electricity bills. Abbott championed data centers for years, took millions from their developers, and is now scrambling to reverse course. Gina called for a moratorium from day one.
As Gina put it to The Nation: The data-center issue is the latest example of a governor doing the bidding of moneyed interests and not the people of Texas. And it is angering MAGA Republicans — not country-club Republicans, not Chamber of Commerce Republicans. There is an opportunity for alliances to be forged when we are pursuing a populist agenda.
**Even Abbott's own team is admitting this race is close.**
Abbott's longtime political strategist was asked about the tightening polls. His response: "Is it going to be close on Election Day? Yes." That’s Abbott's own guy publicly conceding this goes to the wire. And when pressed on his best argument against Gina? He went to culture wars and lies on income tax votes — not data centers, not schools, not the affordability crisis Abbott has presided over for twelve years. When culture wars are the best attack you can come up with, you're losing ground.
**The coalition winning this race doesn't look like past Texas Democratic coalitions.**
Gina leads independents by 38 points in the Siena poll. She's winning women 57–40%, voters under 45 by 60–33%, and Gen Z 71–19%. She's pulling 9% of self-identified Republicans. In TX-15 — a district Trump carried 58–41 — a House Majority PAC poll shows Gina leading 52–47.
This is a cross-partisan, cross-regional majority being built in real time. _Gina is earning support from Texans who have never voted for a Democrat before in their lives._
**When Texas Democrats run strong, the whole map shifts.**
In 2018, when Beto lost the Senate race by just 2.6 points, that wave energy flipped 12 State House seats, 2 State Senate seats, and 2 congressional seats. And the stakes this cycle go even further: if Abbott wins another term, Republicans will redraw the congressional map again. Combined with seats Texas gains after the next Census, that could put nine or ten congressional seats permanently out of Democratic reach — one-party control of Congress, likely for a generation. A governor who vetoes rigged maps changes all of that. As Gina said: _"We flip Texas, and it's over."_
**The bottom line.**
Four polls show Gina leading. One has us tied. Abbott is underwater on favorability and approval. Conservatives are crossing over to support our campaign. The polling average is under 2 points. Abbott's own strategist admits this race will be close.
_This race is winnable._ But Abbott is going to spend over $106 million to try to buy his lead back in the final few weeks of this race.
Gina has raised a fraction of Abbott’s war chest. The only thing that closes the spending gap is donors who understand what's actually happening in Texas right now — and decide this race is worth their investment.
We can win this. But only if people show up.
=============================================================
Peter, I'll leave you with this.
Greg Abbott has been in statewide office for 30 years. He has 98 percent name recognition. He has raised over $106 million to run this campaign. And he still can’t grab onto an insurmountable lead in this race.
Texans know his record. They know who he works for. And they're ready for something different.
The only question is whether we have what it takes to close this out — whether the people who believe Texas can change are willing to put real resources behind it in these final weeks.
We have people working in every corner of this state who are hungry for this. Abbott's own team is bracing for a close race. Four polls have us ahead.
We can win this. But not without you.
**[Will you rush a donation to our campaign right now?](https://act.ginafortexas.com/go/1356?c0=em_ms_gh_20261012_2_memo.mPsRb1&refcode=em20261012-2390&t=3&akid=2390%2E299639%2E85G_us)**
[Donate $5 »](https://act.ginafortexas.com/go/625?c0=em_ms_gh_20261012_2_memo.5iPKWt&amount=5&refcode=em20261012-2390&t=4&akid=2390%2E299639%2E85G_us)
Thank you for believing in what we're building together.
— Gina Hinojosa
Democratic Nominee for Governor of Texas

[ Donate » ](https://secure.actblue.com/donate/em_ms_gh_footer?refcode=em20261012-2&t=5&refcode2=2390_299639_85G_us&akid=2390%2E299639%2E85G_us)
[ Donate Weekly » ](https://secure.actblue.com/donate/em_ms_gh_footer?refcode=em20261012-2&recurring=1&t=6&refcode2=2390_299639_85G_us&akid=2390%2E299639%2E85G_us)
---

Donate By Mail
Gina Hinojosa Campaign

Austin, TX 78703
This email was sent to dpwillis67@gmail.com. Email is the most important way we keep in touch with people like you, so thank you for reading to the end.

This week in Washington, tens of thousands of military leaders, defense executives, investors, and entrepreneurs are gathering for the Association of the United States Army's (AUSA) [annual meeting.](https://substack.com/redirect/35793eec-04e1-411d-a932-211d5ce19bcb?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) The conversations are about America's future: artificial intelligence, autonomous weapons systems, robotics, advanced manufacturing, and the billions of dollars in private capital flowing into a new generation of defense technology companies.
It's an exciting moment for American innovation, particularly for veterans who are increasingly moving from military service into entrepreneurship, investment, and leadership across the defense economy. But as we look toward the future of America's military and economy, it's worth remembering the generation that helped build both.
We know what the Vietnam War cost America - 58,220 never came home. Have we ever fully calculated what Vietnam veterans gave back when they came home?
More than half a century after the last American combat troops departed Vietnam, the numbers remain staggering. According to the Department of Veterans Affairs, approximately 8.7 million Americans served in uniform during the Vietnam era, including roughly 2.7 million who served in Vietnam itself. More than 300,000 were wounded.
These numbers tell us about sacrifice. They do not begin to capture the decades of contributions that followed when they came home.
For many, the homecoming was hardly a hero's welcome. Veterans returned to a country deeply divided over the war, often carrying physical wounds and psychological scars that would take decades for the nation to fully acknowledge.
Yet the generation that America struggled to welcome home went on to help build the America we know today. Too often, Americans failed to separate the war from the warrior.
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, an estimated 5.2 million Vietnam-era veterans were still living in 2023. They represent one of the most influential generations in modern American history, not only because of the war they fought, but because of how they kept America as the world's best economy after returning home.
We have spent decades debating the legacy of the Vietnam War. It's time we paid greater attention to the legacy of the people who served during it and what they accomplished in the decades that followed

## **Their Economic Legacy is Profound**
When Americans think about the Vietnam generation, they often think about the draft, antiwar demonstrations, the fall of Saigon, or the names etched into the Vietnam Veterans Memorial. Far less attention is given to the veterans who returned and helped build the American economy over the next five decades.
Some of the most recognizable companies in America were built by men whose military service shaped their approach to business and leadership.
Take Fred Smith, the founder of FedEx. A Marine Corps officer who served two tours in Vietnam, earning a Bronze Star and two Purple Hearts, Smith founded Federal Express in 1971. His company transformed the movement of goods around the world, creating an entirely new standard for overnight delivery and global logistics. The leadership and logistical experience he developed in the military became part of the foundation of a company that changed American commerce.
And Smith was hardly alone. Some of America's most recognizable companies were built by veterans who served during the Vietnam War or the years surrounding it. They include Phil Knight, founder of Nike; Ralph Lauren, founder of his namesake fashion empire; Richard Kinder, co-founder of Kinder Morgan; Bob Parsons, founder of GoDaddy; and Daniel D'Aniello, co-founder of the Carlyle Group.
Their contributions spanned industries from fashion and finance to energy and technology, demonstrating how military experience could translate into leadership far beyond the armed forces.
These founders are exceptional, but the broader economic contribution of veterans extends well beyond household names. The Census Bureau reported that in 2007, American veterans owned approximately 2.4 million businesses, representing 9 percent of all businesses nationwide. Those businesses generated $1.2 trillion in annual receipts and employed nearly 5.8 million people.
Although those figures include veterans of multiple generations, they illustrate the enormous economic contributions of Americans who served in uniform.
Military service does not guarantee business success, but it can develop traits and skills that are highly valuable in civilian leadership: managing teams, navigating uncertainty, making decisions under pressure, and taking responsibility for outcomes. In fact, veteran-run businesses are more likely to succeed than their civilian counterparts.
For many veterans, however, the transition from military service to entrepreneurship was about more than applying the skills they learned in uniform. It was about finding a new sense of purpose after war.
Bob Parsons, a Vietnam veteran and the founder of GoDaddy, described that transformation when I interviewed him for Warrior Money. He returned home a changed man, carrying an experience that would shape the rest of his life.

## **The Generation That Helped Rebuild the American Army**
The Army being discussed at AUSA this week is profoundly different from the Army that fought in Vietnam. Much of that transformation began with the difficult lessons of the war and the military leaders who lived through it.
In 1973, the United States ended the draft and transitioned to an all-volunteer military. But building a professional, all-volunteer force required rethinking how the Army recruited, trained, and prepared its soldiers for combat.
The decades following Vietnam brought major changes in Army doctrine, including more realistic combat training and a renewed emphasis on readiness. Institutions such as the National Training Center, established at Fort Irwin in 1980, became central to preparing military units for the battlefield. Many of the officers and noncommissioned officers who helped guide these reforms had been shaped by their experiences in Vietnam.
For us this history is personal.
**Patrick:** Two of my uncles served in Vietnam, my father served in the military during the Vietnam War, and I was named after Specialist Patrick Ward, who gave the ultimate sacrifice trying to save others in combat. Years later, I served as an Army officer in Iraq, taught constitutional law at West Point, and eventually became Under Secretary and Acting Secretary of the Army. Throughout my career, I benefited from the professionalism, training standards, and leadership culture that Vietnam veterans helped build. The Army I served in was stronger because of the lessons their generation carried forward.
Their influence also extended to the way America treats those who return from war.
The Department of Veterans Affairs established Vet Centers in 1979 to provide community-based counseling and support to veterans who were not necessarily accessing traditional VA services. Recognition of post-traumatic stress disorder, the long-term consequences of combat exposure, and the health effects associated with Agent Orange became important parts of the national conversation about veterans' care.
Vietnam veterans and their advocates helped push those issues into public view. Their efforts contributed to a more comprehensive understanding of the responsibilities that continue after military service ends.
**Patrick:** What has always stood out to me about Vietnam veterans is how they treated those of us who came home from Iraq and Afghanistan. After being denied the welcome they deserved, they could have turned their backs on our generation. Instead, they were among the first to greet us with the words they had waited decades to hear themselves: "Welcome home, brother. Welcome home, sister."
Since 9/11, we have lost an estimated [140,000 veterans to suicide](https://substack.com/redirect/2fff4087-40e8-4700-a83f-2ed610fe9285?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), a heartbreaking reminder of how much work remains to support those who served. But Vietnam veterans helped ensure that our generation would not face those challenges alone, fighting for better care, greater recognition, and a country that understood its responsibilities did not end when its soldiers came home.
They could not change how America treated them. But they helped change how America treated the veterans who came after them.
## **From Vietnam to the New Defense Economy**
That history makes the conversations happening at AUSA especially relevant.
A recent Forbes feature, _Soldiers With Fortunes_ , examined the extraordinary rise of veteran entrepreneurs in America's defense technology sector. According to figures cited in the article, defense startups attracted approximately $12.8 billion in venture capital during the first half of 2026. Nearly 1,100 defense startups were founded in 2025, almost four times the number founded in 2022.
Although that investment extends beyond veteran-owned companies, it reflects a growing opportunity for former service members to turn their battlefield experience into businesses solving national security challenges.
The Vietnam generation paved the way for our generation's veterans, such as Dino Mavrookas, a former Navy SEAL who cofounded Saronic, an autonomous maritime technology company valued at approximately $9.3 billion earlier this year. Chad McCoy, an Air Force veteran with nearly 23 years of service, cofounded Firestorm Labs, which is developing rapidly manufactured unmanned systems. And beyond defense technology, former Army infantry officer Blake Hall founded ID.me, demonstrating how veterans are applying their experience to challenges across the civilian economy. (Disclosure: Blake is a friend, and our venture capital partners have invested more than $1 million in ID.me.)
Half a century separates these entrepreneurs from the Vietnam generation, but the underlying principle remains the same: Military service can prepare Americans not only to defend their country, but to help build its future.
The challenge now is ensuring that these opportunities reach more than a handful of well-connected founders. Access to capital remains a major obstacle for many veteran entrepreneurs. Government procurement can be difficult to navigate, and promising businesses often struggle to bridge the gap between an innovative idea and a sustainable enterprise.
If we want the next generation of veterans to build on the Vietnam generation's legacy, we must do more to connect their talent with the capital, mentorship, and opportunities needed to succeed.
## **The Return on America 's Investment**
Every year, the United States invests billions of dollars in recruiting, training, educating, and developing the men and women who serve in our armed forces. We measure that investment in readiness, military capability, and operational effectiveness.
But there is another return on that investment that rarely appears in a defense budget.
It's what veterans go on to contribute long after their military service ends. The Vietnam generation helped build some of America's most successful companies, strengthen its institutions, and prepare the next generation of military leaders.
Their service did not end with their discharge papers, and neither did their contributions to the country.
Supporting veterans means more than thanking them for their service. It means giving them the opportunities, resources, and support to thrive long after they leave uniform.
Vietnam veterans spent decades proving what they could do for America. But their worth was never dependent on the businesses they built, the jobs they created, or the institutions they strengthened. Their service alone earned our gratitude and support. And for some, there is still one journey left unfinished.
## **One Mission We Still Have Time to Complete**
With Veterans Day approaching, we have an opportunity to do something meaningful for a generation whose sacrifices and contributions have shaped our country for more than half a century.
Thousands of Vietnam veterans have expressed a desire to return to the country where they once served, not to relive the war, but to honor those they lost and, perhaps, find a measure of peace.
**Genine:** This mission is especially personal to me because of my friendship with Timothy Davis, founder of Vietnam Inc., an organization helping veterans return to Vietnam. Through Tim, I've come to understand how much this journey can mean to men and women who have spent decades carrying memories of the war, the friends they lost, and the places that changed their lives.
Tim speaks about America's responsibility to this generation with an urgency that reflects both his commitment to veterans and the reality that time is running out.
As he puts it:
"We sent them to war when they were young, and too many came home to a country that turned its back on them. They have carried the memories of that war, and the friends they left behind, for more than fifty years. We failed them when we sent them. We failed them when they returned. Now, as they grow old, we have one last chance to do right by them. For God's sake, let's not fail them a third time."
His words confront us with a simple truth: We cannot change what happened to these veterans, but we can still change what happens next.
Through its Return to Vietnam initiative, Vietnam Inc. is helping veterans make a journey some have waited a lifetime to take. Its mission is simple:
"We bring veterans back to the battlefields of their past--not to relive the war, but to find peace with it."
For some veterans, the journey means returning to the place where a friend died. For others, it means seeing a village, a former military installation, or a stretch of countryside they have remembered for decades. For others still, it means seeing Vietnam as a place of peace rather than war.
No journey can erase what happened, and no organization can promise that returning will bring closure. But there is tremendous dignity in allowing these veterans to make that journey on their own terms, with support and understanding.
And time is running out. These veterans are now in their 70s and 80s, and the opportunity to make that journey will not last forever.
We cannot give them back their youth or bring home the friends they lost. Nor can we undo the welcome so many never received.
But we can do this one thing.
We can help them return.
And perhaps, after all these years, we can finally give something back to a generation that gave so much.
They helped build an America that did not always welcome them home. We cannot change that history, but we can still help write a different ending to part of their story.
This Veterans Day, we're asking our friends and colleagues to do more than remember their sacrifice. Help us give these veterans the opportunity to complete a journey that began more than half a century ago.

Patrick: Two of my uncles served in Vietnam, my father served in the military during the Vietnam War, and I was named after Specialist Patrick Ward, who gave the ultimate sacrifice trying to save others in combat. Years later, I served as an Army officer in Iraq, taught constitutional law at West Point, and eventually became Under Secretary and Acting Secretary of the Army. Throughout my career, I benefited from the professionalism, training standards, and leadership culture that Vietnam veterans helped build. The Army I served in was stronger because of the lessons their generation carried forward. Their influence also extended to the way America treats those who return from war. The Department of Veterans Affairs established Vet Centers in 1979 to provide community-based counseling and support to veterans who were not necessarily accessing traditional VA services. Recognition of post-traumatic stress disorder, the long-term consequences of combat exposure, and the health effects associated with Agent Orange became important parts of the national conversation about veterans' care. Vietnam veterans and their advocates helped push those issues into public view. Their efforts contributed to a more comprehensive understanding of the responsibilities that continue after military service ends. Patrick: What has always stood out to me about Vietnam veterans is how they treated those of us who came home from Iraq and Afghanistan. After being denied the welcome they deserved, they could have turned their backs on our generation. Instead, they were among the first to greet us with the words they had waited decades to hear themselves: "Welcome home, brother. Welcome home, sister." Since 9/11, we have lost an estimated , a heartbreaking reminder of how much work remains to support those who served. But Vietnam veterans helped ensure that our generation would not face those challenges alone, fighting for better care, greater recognition, and a country that understood its responsibilities did not end when its soldiers came home. They could not change how America treated them. But they helped change how America treated the veterans who came after them. From Vietnam to the New Defense Economy That history makes the conversations happening at AUSA especially relevant. A recent Forbes feature, Soldiers With Fortunes , examined the extraordinary rise of veteran entrepreneurs in America's defense technology sector. According to figures cited in the article, defense startups attracted approximately $12.8 billion in venture capital during the first half of 2026. Nearly 1,100 defense startups were founded in 2025, almost four times the number founded in 2022. Although that investment extends beyond veteran-owned companies, it reflects a growing opportunity for former service members to turn their battlefield experience into businesses solving national security challenges. The Vietnam generation paved the way for our generation's veterans, such as Dino Mavrookas, a former Navy SEAL who cofounded Saronic, an autonomous maritime technology company valued at approximately $9.3 billion earlier this year. Chad McCoy, an Air Force veteran with nearly 23 years of service, cofounded Firestorm Labs, which is developing rapidly manufactured unmanned systems. And beyond defense technology, former Army infantry officer Blake Hall founded ID.me, demonstrating how veterans are applying their experience to challenges across the civilian economy. (Disclosure: Blake is a friend, and our venture capital partners have invested more than $1 million in ID.me.) Half a century separates these entrepreneurs from the Vietnam generation, but the underlying principle remains the same: Military service can prepare Americans not only to defend their country, but to help build its future. The challenge now is ensuring that these opportunities reach more than a handful of well-connected founders. Access to capital remains a major obstacle for many veteran entrepreneurs. Government procurement can be difficult to navigate, and promising businesses often struggle to bridge the gap between an innovative idea and a sustainable enterprise. If we want the next generation of veterans to build on the Vietnam generation's legacy, we must do more to connect their talent with the capital, mentorship, and opportunities needed to succeed. The Return on America 's Investment Every year, the United States invests billions of dollars in recruiting, training, educating, and developing the men and women who serve in our armed forces. We measure that investment in readiness, military capability, and operational effectiveness. But there is another return on that investment that rarely appears in a defense budget. It's what veterans go on to contribute long after their military service ends. The Vietnam generation helped build some of America's most successful companies, strengthen its institutions, and prepare the next generation of military leaders. Their service did not end with their discharge papers, and neither did their contributions to the country. Supporting veterans means more than thanking them for their service. It means giving them the opportunities, resources, and support to thrive long after they leave uniform. Vietnam veterans spent decades proving what they could do for America. But their worth was never dependent on the businesses they built, the jobs they created, or the institutions they strengthened. Their service alone earned our gratitude and support. And for some, there is still one journey left unfinished. One Mission We Still Have Time to Complete With Veterans Day approaching, we have an opportunity to do something meaningful for a generation whose sacrifices and contributions have shaped our country for more than half a century. Thousands of Vietnam veterans have expressed a desire to return to the country where they once served, not to relive the war, but to honor those they lost and, perhaps, find a measure of peace. Genine: This mission is especially personal to me because of my friendship with Timothy Davis, founder of Vietnam Inc., an organization helping veterans return to Vietnam. Through Tim, I've come to understand how much this journey can mean to men and women who have spent decades carrying memories of the war, the friends they lost, and the places that changed their lives. Tim speaks about America's responsibility to this generation with an urgency that reflects both his commitment to veterans and the reality that time is running out. As he puts it: "We sent them to war when they were young, and too many came home to a country that turned its back on them. They have carried the memories of that war, and the friends they left behind, for more than fifty years. We failed them when we sent them. We failed them when they returned. Now, as they grow old, we have one last chance to do right by them. For God's sake, let's not fail them a third time." His words confront us with a simple truth: We cannot change what happened to these veterans, but we can still change what happens next. Through its Return to Vietnam initiative, Vietnam Inc. is helping veterans make a journey some have waited a lifetime to take. Its mission is simple: "We bring veterans back to the battlefields of their past--not to relive the war, but to find peace with it." For some veterans, the journey means returning to the place where a friend died. For others, it means seeing a village, a former military installation, or a stretch of countryside they have remembered for decades. For others still, it means seeing Vietnam as a place of peace rather than war. No journey can erase what happened, and no organization can promise that returning will bring closure. But there is tremendous dignity in allowing these veterans to make that journey on their own terms, with support and understanding. And time is running out. These veterans are now in their 70s and 80s, and the opportunity to make that journey will not last forever. We cannot give them back their youth or bring home the friends they lost. Nor can we undo the welcome so many never received. But we can do this one thing. We can help them return. And perhaps, after all these years, we can finally give something back to a generation that gave so much. They helped build an America that did not always welcome them home. We cannot change that history, but we can still help write a different ending to part of their story. This Veterans Day, we're asking our friends and colleagues to do more than remember their sacrifice. Help us give these veterans the opportunity to complete a journey that began more than half a century ago. ￼** Learn more about Vietnam Inc.'s mission at. clean_body: | | | = | | On Friday, I visited the Macadam ICE facility alongside my fellow members of Congress to conduct oversight and get answers about what is happening inside. We’ve heard very concerning reports that attorneys are being turned away and prevented from meeting with their clients. Meanwhile, the number of detentions is rapidly escalating, and people are being disappeared; moved past the processing facility in Portland, directly to the NW Detention Facility or other facilities outside of the state very quickly. This facility should be a place where people detained in Oregon receive due process, not one where their rights are denied. Every person in this country has a constitutional right to due process and the right to an attorney. These are fundamental protections for everyone, regardless of immigration status. As a physician and a member of Congress, I believe our government has a responsibility to treat people with dignity and respect their basic rights. We cannot look away when those rights are being denied. Oversight means demanding answers, confronting abuses, and making sure the government is held accountable. I will keep pressing for answers about what is happening with arrests being made by masked, unidentified agents in our community, how due process is being denied inside the Macadam facility, and I will keep showing up to hold our government accountable. | | | | | | Everyone deserves to have their rights respected. No exceptions. Keep the pressure on, Dr. Maxine Dexter | | | | | = | | Maxine Dexter is a critical care physician with decades of experience using facts and following science to help her patients. Now she's using those skills in Congress to ensure healthy communities by standing up to Big Pharma, fighting climate change, and expanding reproductive rights, as well as rebuilding a fair economy for all by protecting Social Security and Medicare. **[Broadcom's Hock Tan and Intel's Lip-Bu Tan](https://substack.com/redirect/e21a4b3d-b643-4090-afb0-3ef1be1f5d81?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** warned at a Singapore conference that **[financing constraints](https://substack.com/redirect/9012c38e-7c81-4d90-85c4-5c47e7da0267?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** may now limit AI expansion more than chip, memory or power shortages.

* **ROI pressure** : Lip-Bu Tan stressed that companies will need to show returns on heavy AI investment as the cost of capital rises.

Dutch TTF futures trade near 83 euros per megawatt-hour, the highest since early 2023, as **[Europe heads into winter](https://substack.com/redirect/9a246077-d2db-4123-9188-53d6474ee752?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** without Qatari LNG even while Citi sees the supply squeeze easing.

* **Prior pressure** : Goldman had earlier said prices near 100 euros might be needed to free Asian cargoes for Europe.

body:
Because health care is a human right.
# [](https://act.pramilaforcongress.com/go/892?refcode=em20261012-6825-footer&t=1&akid=6825%2E420207%2EUbPAFR)
Peter,
**A new poll from the _Wall Street Journal_ shows 59% of Americans support passing Medicare for All:**
[****](https://act.pramilaforcongress.com/go/47393?c0=pj-em-20261012.QgQQA1&refcode=em20261012-6825&amount=3&t=2&akid=6825%2E420207%2EUbPAFR)
This is right in line with our recent independent MFA polling showing 94% of Democrats, 60% of Independents, and 1 in 5 Republicans support Medicare For All.
But despite majority support for the only policy that will _actually_ end medical financial stress and put patients over profits, Trump just announced a short-sighted plan to spend $2 billion sending one-time $90 checks to Medicare enrollees.
And in classic Trump fashion, less than one-third of Medicare recipients are even eligible for this payment. The move also doesn’t address the root causes of rising health care costs: Big Pharma and insurance companies putting profits over people.
This is one of the Trump administration’s many desperate last-minute attempts to hold onto power — but it’s not going to work. Trump’s approval ratings are floundering, and he’s grasping at straws to stay in control.
**Medicare for All is increasingly popular — Trump and MAGA are not.**
I have introduced Medicare for All legislation into every session of Congress, and I will continue to do so until we can guarantee that every single person is guaranteed the health care that they need.
